A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same UnKE method and UnKEBench benchmark despite the changed title. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison. Some inconsistent table labels limit interpretation of particular scores, but do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original UnKEBench and KEBench experiments, human evaluations, and batch, sequential, and decoding-temperature analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical evaluations and reports additional MMLU results, component ablations, layer-selection experiments, and human–automatic evaluation correlations.

M1.justification: The two-stage key optimization, edited Transformer layer, and three loss terms remain equivalent. Key Paraphrase Loss is renamed Key Causal Loss and reinterpreted without changing its objective. Although v2 calls preservation examples 'pre-training samples' in the main text, both implementation appendices specify the same 20 Alpaca instruction examples.

E1.justification: v2 expands evaluation beyond targeted editing to general-ability preservation using MMLU and unrelated subject/object knowledge in KEBench. These introduce substantive coverage of collateral effects. The underlying 1,000-example UnKEBench collection, structured editing datasets, and original/paraphrased question tasks remain.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is retained: Table 2 evaluates FT-A, FT-L, ROME, MEMIT, and MEND on LLaMA, and MEMIT on Qwen. Human and structured evaluations retain their existing comparator subsets. Newly discussed methods such as PMET, KEP, and EVEDIT are not added as evaluated competitors.

E3.justification: v2 introduces five randomly sampled MMLU questions per editing example, hierarchical score averaging, unedited-model reference scores, and Src-Acc/Tgt-Acc locality metrics. New experiments vary optimized modules, loss components, and layers L=5–12. The temperature sweep is removed. Main model sizes, single-edit decoding temperature, and human-evaluation sample and rater counts remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds module and loss ablations, UnKE layer sensitivity, human–automatic metric correlations, and an UnKEBench extension of MEMIT's layer analysis. These test component necessity, layer choice, and evaluation validity. v1's decoding-temperature robustness analysis is removed; batch/sequential analyses and the generation case study are retained, with several moved to appendices.

E5.justification: v2 adds Pearson correlation estimation and associated p-values in Appendix G, including explicit significance interpretation. This statistical addition is confined to metric validation. Human-rating averaging and Fleiss' kappa of 0.57 remain unchanged; neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty for the main performance results.

E6.justification: Reported UnKE FactScore on LLaMA changes from 38.82 to 42.49, and KEBench Ori-Acc/Para-Acc changes from 87.60/70.40 to 94.30/86.40. Batch-editing values are extensively replaced, and MMLU, locality, ablation, layer-sensitivity, and correlation results are added. Temperature results disappear. Metric assignments conflict across v2 Tables 2, 4, 7, and 8, so not every apparent score change supports a reliable performance comparison.

T1.justification: v2's explicit key/value equations restate definitions already present in v1, and the optimization objectives remain mathematically equivalent after notation changes. The labeled hypotheses are empirical motivations, not new formal assumptions or proofs. No substantive theoretical result is added or removed.

C1.justification: Both versions claim an unstructured editing benchmark, a method extending local and term-based editing, superior structured/unstructured editing performance, and robust batch/sequential editing. The new title, terminology, and abstract emphasis do not materially change these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 reinterprets the middle loss as preserving context rather than promoting paraphrase generalization, and develops an early-decoding explanation for the shallow/deep layer split. It adds interpretations of component ablations, deeper-layer failure, general-ability preservation, and metric correlations. Removing the temperature study also removes its argument that UnKE learns semantics rather than memorizing.

D1.justification: v2 newly specifies that human annotators were uninvolved in the project's training and documents the MMLU scoring implementation and aggregation. The detailed optimizer settings, learning rates, optimization steps, Alpaca sampling, hardware, runtimes, and repository access information are retained from v1, largely through relocation to Appendix H.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around localization critiques, attention-layer knowledge, and early decoding, citing Hase, Li, Wei, Wang, and Yao. Appendix A adds substantive distinctions from KEP and EVEDIT and expands the Eva-KELLM comparison. These additions strengthen discussion of both the method's motivation and the benchmark's relationship to prior work.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, motivation, and method exposition are extensively rewritten. Method subsections are reorganized around block key-value storage and causal optimization; explicit contribution bullets disappear. Experiments are regrouped, while baseline descriptions and batch/sequential analysis move into an expanded appendix structure.

P2.justification: v2 revises Figure 1's annotations and redraws Figure 2 with structured/unstructured curves and dual axes. It adds ablation, layer-selection, and correlation tables, expands existing tables with preservation metrics, removes the temperature table, and relocates robustness displays. Typography, headers, spacing, and table-column arrangements also change substantially.

improvement.justification: v2 supplies useful evidence missing from v1 about component necessity, layer selection, and collateral effects, while clarifying the method and quantifying human–automatic agreement. These improve empirical scrutiny. However, inconsistent metric assignments across Tables 2, 4, 7, and 8, unexplained replacements of main scores, and removal of temperature-robustness evidence limit the gain. The net improvement is modest.
